text: matplotlib and seaborn produce static images. Plotly produces interactive charts: hover for exact values, drag to zoom, click a legend entry to hide a group. That makes it a great fit for exploration and for dashboards people will poke at themselves, and because it's just a web page, you can share it as one HTML file.

Plotly Express, imported as px, feels like seaborn: pass a DataFrame, name the columns. One function call gives you a complete interactive chart. On the 300-row retail table, px dot scatter takes x, y, and color as column names, hover_data adds extra columns to the tooltip, and category_orders fixes the legend and color order.

Hovering over any point in the real chart shows its orders, spend, age and region, and you can drag to zoom into the dense cluster of customers with three to seven orders. That's the whole point of an interactive chart: the reader explores it themselves.

update_traces changes the marks, like marker size and opacity. update_layout changes the chart as a whole: template, legend title, axis titles. fig dot show displays it inline or in a browser. write_html saves a shareable page that works offline, though it embeds the whole Plotly library, so it's over a megabyte.

To save a static image instead, for a slide or PDF, fig dot write_image works once the kaleido package is installed. That's exactly how this lesson's own screenshot was produced: the real interactive chart, exported flat.

Every other Plotly Express function shares the same shape: a DataFrame, column names for x, y, color, and a few options. px dot line, px dot histogram, px dot box, and px dot bar. Learn scatter and you've learned all of them.

Choose interactive when you're exploring or when stakeholders will slice and zoom themselves. Choose static for a printed report or one clear takeaway. Interactivity never replaces good design. Next lesson: subplots and dashboards in Python.
